meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You Don't Have to Know Everything. You Just Have to Know Where to Find It'?
meta.ogDescription: Johnson's real 1775 line was worded differently. The sentence people quote comes from John Brunner's novel The Shockwave Rider (1975).

answer.label: Not Samuel Johnson — actually John Brunner
answer.sourceLine: Johnson said something close, but not this. In April 1775, browsing a friend’s library, he told the room that “Knowledge is of two kinds. We know a subject ourselves, or we know where we can find information upon it” (Boswell’s Life of Johnson). The compressed modern sentence belongs to the science-fiction writer John Brunner: the earliest exact match in Quote Investigator’s chronology is a line of dialogue in his 1975 novel The Shockwave Rider.

source.excerpt: Ah, you don’t have to know everything. You just have to know where to find it.
trail: 1775 — At Mr. Cambridge’s villa on the Thames near Twickenham, Johnson makes straight for the bookshelves and, challenged about it, replies: “Knowledge is of two kinds. We know a subject ourselves, or we know where we can find information upon it.” Boswell dates the visit Tuesday, 18 April 1775 (Life of Johnson).

1921 — In Boston, Einstein is asked the speed of sound and declines to answer, saying the figure is readily available in textbooks; a fuller telling published in 1947 has him say he does not burden his memory with facts he can find in any textbook. This is the root of the Einstein version (Quote Investigator).
1968 — John Brunner gives a character in Stand on Zanzibar the near-final form: “You don’t have to know everything. You simply need to know where to find it when necessary.” (Quote Investigator)
1975 — Brunner returns to the line in The Shockwave Rider, in the form that circulates today — the earliest exact match in QI’s chronology.
source.excerptNote: A line of dialogue in Brunner’s 1975 novel, transcribed by Quote Investigator from page 75 of the Del Rey/Ballantine printing. Brunner had used a near-identical line seven years earlier in Stand on Zanzibar.

author.name: John Brunner
author.kicker: The man who actually wrote the line
author.heading: Who was John Brunner?
author.metaLine: 1934–1995 · British science-fiction novelist · Hugo Award winner
author.bio: John Kilian Houston Brunner was a prolific British science-fiction writer whose bleak, prophetic novels of the late 1960s and 1970s — Stand on Zanzibar, The Sheep Look Up, The Shockwave Rider — extrapolated overpopulation, ecological collapse and the networked society. Stand on Zanzibar won the Hugo Award for Best Novel in 1969. The Shockwave Rider is best remembered for coining the computing sense of “worm” — and, in passing, for a throwaway line about knowledge that long ago outran its author’s name.

misattribution.heading: Two big names, neither of them the author
misattribution.intro: This sentence travels under two famous names, and the record supports neither for this wording.

items.why: Johnson really did say that knowledge is of two kinds — knowing a subject, or knowing where to find information on it — at Mr. Cambridge’s villa on 18 April 1775, as Boswell records. But the compressed modern sentence is not in Boswell, and Wikiquote’s sourced Johnson list carries only the 1775 wording.

Aggregators still print “I don’t need to know everything, I just need to know where to find it, when I need it” over Einstein’s name (AZQuotes). Quote Investigator found no matching line in his writings and notes it is absent from Princeton’s The Ultimate Quotable Einstein; what Einstein actually did, in Boston in 1921, was decline to state the speed of sound because the figure was available in any textbook (Quote Investigator).

misattribution.truthLine: The exact sentence is documented in John Brunner’s 1975 novel The Shockwave Rider — the earliest exact match in Quote Investigator’s chronology, which runs from Johnson in 1775 through several looser variants to Brunner.

context.heading: Why Johnson gets the credit
lead: The thought is genuinely Johnson’s, and older than the internet by two centuries. On Tuesday 18 April 1775, Boswell and Sir Joshua Reynolds took Johnson to dine at Mr. Cambridge’s villa on the Thames near Twickenham. Johnson made straight for the bookshelves; when his host remarked that it seemed odd to want to look at the backs of books, Johnson — “ever ready for contest” — wheeled round and delivered the answer that has been quoted ever since (Life of Johnson).

What changed was the packaging. Johnson’s two-part sentence is an argument about catalogues and libraries; the modern one-liner is a slogan for the search-engine age, and it arrives fully formed in a 1975 novel about a man on the run through a national data network. That the same page of thinking should be credited to a lexicographer of 1775 and to a physicist who died in 1955 says more about how quotations travel than about who wrote them.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology records the idea surfacing repeatedly in different words: a 1914 advertisement in The Expositor and Current Anecdotes holding that educated people are those who know where to find information at a moment’s notice, a similar remark in The Post Magazine and Insurance Monitor in 1917, and the social reformer Sophonisba Breckinridge telling her University of Chicago students, in an account published in 1958, that they did not have to know everything but should learn how and where to find what they needed (Quote Investigator).

Brunner used the idea twice. A character in Stand on Zanzibar (1968) says you do not have to know everything, you simply need to know where to find it when necessary; the tighter version that circulates today appears in The Shockwave Rider seven years later.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's chronology of this saying includes Johnson's 1775 remark, Einstein's 1921 speed-of-sound reply, Breckinridge in 1958, Brunner's Stand on Zanzibar (1968) variant, and the exact wording "Ah, you don't have to know everything. You just have to know where to find it." in The Shockwave Rider (1975, page 75 of the Del Rey/Ballantine printing); it also states the Einstein sayings are not in The Ultimate Quotable Einstein.

Boswell's text records the visit to Mr. Cambridge's villa on the Thames near Twickenham as 'On Tuesday, April 18' [1775] and transcribes Johnson's reply: 'Knowledge is of two kinds. We know a subject ourselves, or we know where we can find information upon it. When we enquire into any subject, the first thing we have to do is to know what books have treated of it. This leads us to look at catalogues, and the backs of books in libraries.'

Wikiquote's Samuel Johnson page lists 'Knowledge is of two kinds. We know a subject ourselves, or we know where we can find information upon it.' among sourced quotations from Boswell's Life of Samuel Johnson, dated 18 April 1775, and contains no entry resembling 'You don't have to know everything. You just have to know where to find it.'
A Samuel Johnson quotation site reproduces the full passage, dates it April 18, 1775, and describes the setting as the library at Richard Owen Cambridge's villa.
The Shockwave Rider is a 1975 science-fiction novel by John Brunner, first published by Harper & Row, credited with coining the computing sense of 'worm'.

John Brunner (John Kilian Houston Brunner) was a British science-fiction author, born 24 September 1934, died 25 August 1995, who won the Hugo Award for Best Novel in 1969 for Stand on Zanzibar and wrote The Sheep Look Up (1972) and The Shockwave Rider (1975).
AZQuotes credits Albert Einstein with 'I don't need to know everything, I just need to know where to find it, when I need it.'
